1 Introduction

Workflow tutorial, not publication evidence. This executable vignette uses 150 training samples, 21 aligned validation samples, and the first 100 features from each of the CyTOF and Proteomics assays. Compact lambda grids, small bootstrap counts, and random-permutation decoys keep package builds bounded and catch API drift without optional knockoff dependencies.

A multi-omic dataset is a set of partial views. One assay captures immune-cell state. Another captures circulating proteins. The phenotype is the same individual seen through both. The statistical question is not only which features are stable. It is also whether a feature remains useful when another view can contribute.

This vignette uses a real Onset of Labor (OOL) dataset bundled with stablr. It contains two omic layers, CyTOF and Proteomics, measured in pregnant women. The outcome is days-to-onset-of-labor (DOS), a continuous regression target. The settings stay small for package builds. They still preserve the shape of a real train/validation analysis.

The workflow is as follows:

  1. Load the bundled example data with load_ool_data().
  2. Run per-omic STABL — a useful baseline before integration.
  3. Run the integrated multi-omic workflow with early fusion and late fusion.
  4. Compare selected feature names across strategies.
  5. Export results.

2 Learning objectives

After working through this vignette the reader should be able to:

  1. Understand the data structure returned by load_ool_data().
  2. Run STABL independently on each omic and interpret the outputs.
  3. Explain the difference between early fusion and late fusion.
  4. Run stabl_multiomic_train_validate() and navigate its result list.
  5. Compare which features appear across integration strategies.
  6. Export results for downstream use.

Attach the package as follows.

library(stablr)

3 Loading the data

load_ool_data() reads the bundled OOL subset directly from the package. You need no file paths. It returns a named list with two elements:

  • $x_list: a named list of feature matrices, one per omic layer. Each matrix has samples in rows and features in columns, with matching row names.
  • $y: a named numeric vector of outcomes (DOS in days), aligned to the rows of every matrix in $x_list.

Relation to the Python tutorial notebook. This is a bounded package example, not a full reproduction of Notebook examples/Tutorial Notebook.ipynb. The notebook uses the full OOL-CV training files (CyTOF, Proteomics, and Metabolomics) and the COVID-19 proteomics classification dataset. It also applies a preprocessing pipeline before STABL: zero-variance filtering, high-missingness feature filtering, median imputation, and standardisation. Here, load_ool_data() ships 150 training samples and 21 aligned validation samples for CyTOF and Proteomics only. It keeps the first 100 features from each assay. The matrices are already aligned and have no missing values. These are quick-build settings, not the predeclared full OOL parity analysis. Use docs/PYTHON_TO_R_MAPPING.md when the goal is to mirror the tutorial notebook’s datasets and preprocessing choices.

Load the training and validation splits. Then inspect their dimensions as follows.

ool_train <- load_ool_data(split = "train")
ool_valid <- load_ool_data(split = "valid")

# Training set dimensions
lapply(ool_train$x_list, dim)
#> $cytof
#> [1] 150 100
#> 
#> $proteomics
#> [1] 150 100
length(ool_train$y)
#> [1] 150

# Validation set dimensions
lapply(ool_valid$x_list, dim)
#> $cytof
#> [1]  21 100
#> 
#> $proteomics
#> [1]  21 100

The lapply(..., dim) output confirms the basic geometry: the omics share rows but differ in columns. Row names must match across views. stablr checks this alignment and stops early if it detects a mismatch.

The next chunk summarises the outcome distribution.

# Outcome distribution (DOS = days before onset of labor)
summary(ool_train$y)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#> -113.00  -70.75  -35.50  -43.39  -15.00    0.00

The summary() output shows the spread of DOS. Expect a wide range. A strong skew or a narrow range changes how much prediction signal you can expect from molecular measurements.

4 Per-omic STABL

4.1 Rationale

Analyse each view separately before you integrate the views. A per-omic fit serves as both a sanity check and a baseline:

  1. Sanity check — whether each omic contains any signal at all. If STABL selects zero features from an omic, that layer may not contribute useful information to the integrated analysis.
  2. Baseline — compare the per-omic biomarker lists with the integrated results. This shows which features survive the joint analysis.

This vignette uses compact 6-point lambda grids and small bootstrap counts throughout. For publication-quality results, use 500-1000 bootstraps and broader grids.

In each printed fit, the number of selected feature names and the FDP+ estimate deserve first attention. The ideal result is not a long list. It is a compact list. Decoy features must not explain its stability easily.

4.2 Model fitting

We build a compact lambda grid for the CyTOF view.

lambda_cytof <- auto_lambda_grid(
  ool_train$x_list$cytof, ool_train$y,
  family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 6
)

We fit STABL to the CyTOF view with 10 bootstrap replicates.

fit_cytof <- stabl_fit(
  x               = ool_train$x_list$cytof,
  y               = ool_train$y,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_cytof,
  family          = "gaussian",
  n_bootstraps    = 10L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  random_state    = 42L
)
fit_cytof
#> <stabl_fit>
#>   Features in:      100 
#>   Features selected: 0 
#>   Min FDP+:         1.044 
#>   FDP+ threshold:   1 
#>   Artificial:       random_permutation

We standardise the Proteomics matrix with scale(). Then we compute its lambda grid and fit.

proteomics_train_scaled <- scale(ool_train$x_list$proteomics)
lambda_prot <- auto_lambda_grid(
  proteomics_train_scaled, ool_train$y,
  family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 6
)

fit_prot <- stabl_fit(
  x               = proteomics_train_scaled,
  y               = ool_train$y,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_prot,
  family          = "gaussian",
  n_bootstraps    = 10L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  random_state    = 42L
)
fit_prot
#> <stabl_fit>
#>   Features in:      100 
#>   Features selected: 0 
#>   Min FDP+:         1.01 
#>   FDP+ threshold:   1 
#>   Artificial:       random_permutation

4.3 Selected features and stability paths

The next chunk prints the selected feature names of each omic.

cat("CyTOF selected feature names:\n")
#> CyTOF selected feature names:
print(get_feature_names(fit_cytof))
#> character(0)

cat("\nProteomics selected feature names:\n")
#> 
#> Proteomics selected feature names:
print(get_feature_names(fit_prot))
#> character(0)

get_feature_names() returns the feature names that passed the stability threshold in each omic. get_support() returns the named logical mask for subsetting. Non-overlapping lists suggest view-specific information. Overlap is stronger evidence when the same molecule is present in both layers. The signal has then appeared twice through different measurement systems.

In the stability path, each line is one feature. Features that hold high selection frequencies across a moderate penalty range are the most convincing. Features that appear only when the penalty is very weak are easier to dismiss as opportunistic.

plot_stabl_path(fit_cytof,     title = "CyTOF - stability path")

plot_stabl_path(fit_prot,      title = "Proteomics - stability path")

5 Integrated multi-omic workflow

5.1 Fusion strategies

stabl_multiomic_train_validate() performs the train/validation analysis in one call. It accepts matched omic matrices and evaluates two complementary ways to let the views interact:

Strategy How it works Best when
Early fusion Concatenates all omic matrices into one wide matrix, then runs a single STABL fit across all features jointly. Omics are measured on the same samples; you want a unified biomarker list.
Late fusion Fits one STABL + downstream model per omic separately, learns stacking weights from OOF predictions by default, and applies the weighted blend to full-refit validation predictions. You want a held-out evaluation of an omic-weighted prediction rule.

5.2 Function arguments

Argument Purpose
x_train_list / x_valid_list Named lists of feature matrices; names must match between train and valid.
lambda_grid Named list of lambda grids, one per omic (names must match x_train_list).
early_fusion / late_fusion Toggle each strategy on or off independently.
late_fusion_training Use leakage-safe "oof" (default), or explicit "python_legacy" compatibility mode.
late_fusion_nfolds Number of stacking folds; five folds plus the full refit cost roughly six complete fits.
n_iter_lf Number of optimisation iterations for the late-fusion weight search.

The printed multi_fit object summarises every active branch. You see per-omic selected-feature counts, validation-data presence, early-fusion branch presence, and the late-fusion score. In OOF mode, assessment samples and their groups never enter selector or downstream-model fitting. Use $oof_predictions and $oof_score. Explicit "python_legacy" mode instead exposes $in_sample_predictions and $in_sample_score. The older $train_predictions and $score fields are exact 0.1.x compatibility aliases for the active mode. Binary and regression late fusion use parity-preserving batched stacking. Multiclass stacking remains scalar by design. This preserves probability-normalisation and tie behavior.

5.3 Fitting the joint workflow

We build the per-omic lambda grids from the training data.

# Build per-omic lambda grids
lambda_list <- list(
  cytof      = auto_lambda_grid(ool_train$x_list$cytof,
                                ool_train$y, family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 6),
  proteomics = auto_lambda_grid(ool_train$x_list$proteomics,
                                ool_train$y, family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 6)
)

If you plan cross-validation with stabl_multiomic_cv(), prefer lambda_grid = "auto" or derive grids from training data only. A grid computed on the full dataset leaks mild information into the cross-validated estimates. "auto" avoids this. It builds each fold’s grid from its training data alone.

We run the integrated workflow with both fusion strategies enabled.

multi_fit <- stabl_multiomic_train_validate(
  x_train_list    = ool_train$x_list,
  y_train         = ool_train$y,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_list,
  x_valid_list    = ool_valid$x_list,
  y_valid         = ool_valid$y,
  family          = "gaussian",
  n_bootstraps    = 10L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  early_fusion    = TRUE,
  late_fusion     = TRUE,
  n_iter_lf       = 100L,
  random_state    = 42L
)

multi_fit
#> <stabl_multiomic_fit>
#>   Omics:           2 (cytof, proteomics)
#>   Per-omic selected features:
#>     cytof: 0
#>     proteomics: 0
#>   Validation data:  yes 
#>   Early fusion:     yes (0 features selected) 
#>   Late fusion:      yes (score = 0.1901)

The printed summary lists the active branches of the workflow together with their selected-feature counts and the late-fusion score.

6 Exploring the results

6.1 Elements of the result list

multi_fit is a list because the workflow has several branches. The main elements are:

  • $fits: named list of stabl_fit objects, one per omic. These are the per-omic STABL results produced within the joint pipeline.
  • $early_fusion: result of the early-fusion step (if early_fusion = TRUE), containing $fit (a stabl_fit on the concatenated matrix).
  • $late_fusion: result of the late-fusion step (if late_fusion = TRUE), containing $valid_predictions (validation predictions) and $weights (training-stack model weights).

6.2 Per-omic selected features

The next chunk prints the per-omic selected feature names from the joint pipeline.

# Per-omic selected feature names from the joint pipeline
cat("CyTOF (from multi-omic pipeline):\n")
#> CyTOF (from multi-omic pipeline):
print(get_feature_names(multi_fit$fits$cytof))
#> character(0)

cat("\nProteomics (from multi-omic pipeline):\n")
#> 
#> Proteomics (from multi-omic pipeline):
print(get_feature_names(multi_fit$fits$proteomics))
#> character(0)

These lists come from the fits within the joint pipeline. Compare them with the standalone per-omic results of Section 4.

6.3 Early fusion

The chunk prints the early-fusion selected feature names when the branch is active.

# Early fusion: joint selection across all omics simultaneously
if (!is.null(multi_fit$early_fusion)) {
  cat("Early fusion selected feature names:\n")
  print(get_feature_names(multi_fit$early_fusion$fit))
}
#> Early fusion selected feature names:
#> character(0)

Early fusion can disagree with the per-omic lists because the joint model sees all features at once. A feature that is useful alone may become redundant when another omic carries the same information. This is a property of the joint question, not a failure of the method.

6.4 Late fusion

The next chunk inspects the late-fusion validation predictions.

# Late fusion: weighted blend learned on training predictions and applied to validation samples
if (!is.null(multi_fit$late_fusion)) {
  cat("Late fusion validation predictions (first 6):\n")
  print(head(multi_fit$late_fusion$valid_predictions))
}
#> Late fusion validation predictions (first 6):
#>  004_31_A  004_34_B  015_30_A  015_34_B  015_36_C  047_26_A 
#> -43.39333 -43.39333 -43.39333 -43.39333 -43.39333 -43.39333

$valid_predictions is a numeric vector of predicted DOS values for the held-out validation set, one prediction per sample. Compare these values with ool_valid$y to assess predictive performance. The scatter below makes that comparison direct: points near the identity line indicate calibrated held-out predictions.

lf_df <- data.frame(observed  = ool_valid$y,
                    predicted = multi_fit$late_fusion$valid_predictions)
ggplot2::ggplot(lf_df, ggplot2::aes(observed, predicted)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Late fusion - validation predictions",
                x = "Observed DOS (days)", y = "Predicted DOS (days)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

On these compact build settings the scatter has an honest lesson: the blended predictor is nearly constant (the points form a horizontal line at the training-mean level). Ten bootstraps and six-lambda grids demonstrate the workflow shape, not a competitive prediction rule; run hundreds of bootstraps before reading predictive performance from this figure.

The $weights element records the omic weights chosen by the training-prediction stacking objective. A small weight means that a view received little weight in this fitted prediction rule. It does not mean that the assay is biologically uninformative.

6.5 Stability paths

The next chunk plots the stability paths of the per-omic fits from the joint pipeline.

plot_stabl_path(multi_fit$fits$cytof,
                title = "CyTOF (multi-omic pipeline)")

plot_stabl_path(multi_fit$fits$proteomics,
                title = "Proteomics (multi-omic pipeline)")

These paths correspond to the per-omic fits produced within the joint pipeline.

7 Exporting results

save_stabl_results() writes the result of a single stabl_fit object to disk:

File Content
STABL scores.csv Full stability-score matrix.
Max STABL scores.csv Per-feature maximum stability scores.
FDR Graph.<fmt> FDP diagnostic plot when artificial features are used.
Stability Path.<fmt> Stability path plot.
Selected Features/Selected features.csv Features above the threshold.
Selected Features/Feature distributions.<fmt> Per-feature outcome distributions when features are selected.

Set override = TRUE to overwrite an existing directory. This is useful when you rerun an analysis with more bootstraps or a revised grid.

We export the CyTOF fit from the joint pipeline to a temporary directory.

out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "stablr_ool_cytof")

save_stabl_results(
  object    = multi_fit$fits$cytof,
  path      = out_dir,
  x         = ool_train$x_list$cytof,
  y         = ool_train$y,
  task_type  = "regression",
  figure_fmt = "png",
  override   = TRUE
)

list.files(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
#> [1] "FDR Graph.png"                          
#> [2] "Max STABL artificial scores.csv"        
#> [3] "Max STABL scores.csv"                   
#> [4] "Selected Features/Selected features.csv"
#> [5] "Stability Path.png"                     
#> [6] "STABL artificial scores.csv"            
#> [7] "STABL scores.csv"

The file listing shows the exported score tables, the stability path, and the selected-feature table.

8 Next steps

  • Use stabl_multiomic_cv() for a fully cross-validated evaluation when no pre-defined validation split is available.
  • Pass groups_train (for stabl_multiomic_train_validate()) or groups (for stabl_multiomic_cv()) to respect subject-level grouping in bootstrap resampling and CV fold construction.
  • See vignette("stablr-intro") for single-omic usage and alternative learners.
  • See vignette("stablr-cooperative") for cross-view cooperative fusion (rho tuning) when blocks should agree without full concatenation.
  • For integrative classification benchmarks against mixOmics DIABLO on TCGA, see vignette("stablr-tcga-nestedcv") and inst/analysis/BENCHMARK_PLAN.md.
  • For selection parity with the original Python STABL implementation, see docs/PYTHON_TO_R_MAPPING.md.
